concepts.name: Purpose of feedback
concepts.summary: Explain that feedback exists to help someone continue or improve specific behaviours and results, not to judge or punish the person.

concepts.name: Positive versus constructive feedback
concepts.summary: Recognise the difference between feedback that reinforces what worked and feedback that redirects what should change.

concepts.name: Behaviour versus personality
concepts.summary: Distinguish observable behaviour from assumptions about character and explain why feedback should address only the former.

concepts.name: Specific and timely feedback
concepts.summary: Describe why feedback should cite concrete examples and be given soon after the event.

concepts.name: Listening to feedback openly
concepts.summary: Understand that receiving feedback starts with listening, clarifying and thanking rather than arguing or explaining away.

concepts.name: Private versus public setting
concepts.summary: Remember that corrective feedback is normally given privately while praise can often be shared publicly.

misconceptions.text: Feedback means criticism of what someone did wrong.
Telling someone they are careless or lazy counts as clear feedback.
Receiving feedback means I must explain why I acted as I did.

concepts.name: Separating facts from interpretations
concepts.summary: Rewrite judgemental statements into neutral, observable descriptions before delivering them.

concepts.name: Situation-Behaviour-Impact model
concepts.summary: Structure a feedback message by naming the situation, the observed behaviour and its impact on others or results.

concepts.name: Preparing a feedback conversation
concepts.summary: Gather examples, clarify the desired outcome and choose time and place before holding a conversation.

concepts.name: Asking clarifying questions
concepts.summary: Use open questions to check understanding of feedback received and to invite the other person's view.

concepts.name: Managing defensive reactions
concepts.summary: Notice common defensive responses in yourself and others and respond calmly without escalating.

concepts.name: Turning feedback into actions
concepts.summary: Convert feedback received or given into one or two concrete next steps with a follow-up point.

misconceptions.text: The feedback sandwich of praise, criticism, praise is always the best way to deliver a hard message.
If my intention was good, the impact on the other person does not matter.
Defensiveness from the other person means the feedback was wrong or badly given.

concepts.name: Adapting feedback to the person
concepts.summary: Adjust tone, directness and framing to the individual's experience, motivation and preferences while keeping the message intact.

concepts.name: Feedback versus coaching
concepts.summary: Analyse when to give direct feedback and when to use coaching questions so the person finds their own solution.

concepts.name: Forward-looking feedback
concepts.summary: Analyse how to pair a description of past behaviour with clear expectations and requests for future behaviour.

concepts.name: Building a feedback rhythm
concepts.summary: Embed frequent informal feedback and one-to-ones so formal reviews contain no surprises.

concepts.name: Handling emotional reactions
concepts.summary: Diagnose what drives a strong emotional reaction and decide whether to pause, acknowledge or continue the conversation.

concepts.name: Seeking feedback actively
concepts.summary: Ask specific, well-targeted questions of peers, reports and managers to gather useful input on your own work.

concepts.name: Filtering feedback for value
concepts.summary: Separate useful signal from bias, vague comments and unreliable sources when interpreting feedback you receive.

misconceptions.text: Being kind means softening feedback until the problem is no longer clear.
Annual reviews are enough, since regular feedback just adds noise.
All feedback I receive should be acted on, regardless of who gave it.

concepts.name: Diagnosing root causes of performance
concepts.summary: Determine whether a performance gap stems from skill, motivation, clarity, resources or context before choosing the feedback approach.

concepts.name: Feedback in psychological safety
concepts.summary: Evaluate how team norms, leader reactions and power differences affect whether people give and accept honest feedback.

concepts.name: Difficult and high-stakes conversations
concepts.summary: Plan and judge the approach for conversations involving repeated issues, strong disagreement or serious consequences.

concepts.name: Upward and peer feedback
concepts.summary: Choose and justify how to give feedback to managers and peers where there is no formal authority.

concepts.name: Cross-cultural feedback differences
concepts.summary: Analyse how cultural norms about directness, hierarchy and face change how feedback is given and interpreted.

concepts.name: Bias in feedback
concepts.summary: Identify patterns such as recency, halo and gendered language that distort feedback and correct for them.

concepts.name: Assessing feedback effectiveness
concepts.summary: Judge whether a feedback conversation changed behaviour and trust, and refine the approach accordingly.

misconceptions.text: Poor performance is always a motivation problem that feedback alone can fix.
Direct feedback works the same way in every culture and team.
Objective-sounding feedback is free from bias.

concepts.name: Evaluating 360-degree feedback
concepts.summary: Critically assess the validity, risks and appropriate uses of multi-rater feedback instruments and their results.

concepts.name: Developing feedback capability in others
concepts.summary: Create programmes, practice and coaching that build feedback skill and norms across managers and teams.

concepts.name: Repairing trust after harmful feedback
concepts.summary: Evaluate damage from poorly delivered feedback and choose repair actions that restore the relationship.

concepts.name: Linking feedback to performance decisions
concepts.summary: Judge how developmental feedback should relate to ratings, pay and promotion without undermining candour.

concepts.name: Designing organisational feedback systems
concepts.summary: Design review cycles, peer input and upward channels that fit an organisation's goals, size and culture.

concepts.name: Modelling a learning culture
concepts.summary: Create visible leadership habits of seeking, receiving and acting on feedback that shape norms across the organisation.

misconceptions.text: A formal feedback programme or tool alone creates a feedback culture.
Combining development feedback with ratings and pay makes it more honest.
Once trust is damaged by feedback, nothing can restore it.
